prize_parts.citation: for the proposal and experimental realisation of quantum simulation of lattice many-body models, in particular the Bose-Hubbard model, with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration changes in its credit but not in its subject. After round 1 I think the achievement can be named in one sentence: ultracold atoms in an optical lattice were shown, by proposal and then by experiment, to be a controllable realisation of the Bose-Hubbard model, with the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition as the decisive demonstration. The theory origin is the Jaksch-Zoller proposal, and the experimental origin is the 2002 Mott-insulator experiment of Greiner with Bloch, followed by Bloch's programme that turned the platform into a general instrument with tunable interactions and later single-site readout. I now credit Bloch, Greiner and Zoller instead of Bloch, Cirac and Zoller. Eriksson asked me to name the single achievement and the three decisive people, and Johansson argued that if simulation is chosen the experimental slots matter most; both pushed me toward the lattice proposal and the first many-body experiment rather than the broader Cirac-Zoller quantum-simulation programme. This also loosens the link with the trapped-ion entry, because the decisive theory for this achievement is the lattice proposal and not the Cirac-Zoller gate. The case rests on a theoretical idea becoming a laboratory method that many independent groups have reproduced for over two decades, and on the fact that it changed how many-body problems in statistical and condensed-matter physics are posed.
statement.case_against: The credit is still not clean. The configuration leaves out Cirac, whose proposals for engineered Hamiltonians and quantum simulation were broad, and Dalibard, and I cannot show from the supplied material that Zoller rather than Cirac is the better single theory name for the lattice proposal; Jaksch, a co-author of the key proposal, is not among the credited names at all. The 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize on control of single quantum systems sit nearby, which a critic can use to call the novelty incremental. Analogue simulation has not yet clearly produced results beyond classical simulability, so a harsh reading says this is a mature method whose scientific payoff is still partly in the future. The first-place support for it is narrow, and I should not mistake my own field proximity (many-body models and statistical physics) for evidence of broad support.

responses.point: Eriksson asked me to name the single achievement and the three people whose contribution is decisive, said he finds the experimental realisation more compelling than the proposals, and doubts that this beats B050.
responses.response: I take the challenge seriously and have changed the configuration because of it. The single achievement is Bose-Hubbard simulation with atoms in optical lattices, shown by the Mott-insulator transition; the three decisive names are Zoller for the lattice proposal, and Greiner and Bloch for the experiment and the platform that followed. I agree the experimental side is what makes this a discovery. Whether it beats B050 I cannot say it does on the conceptual criterion; B050 is a sharper prediction-and-measurement pair. My difficulty with B050 remains the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, which you also call unresolved, and I would accept it if the committee finds a defensible reading of the credit.

responses.point: Johansson argued that B015 and B027 share the Cirac-Zoller theory and are not independent options, and that if the committee prefers simulation, Bloch should take the experimental slot over Blatt.
responses.response: The overlap is real and I accept it. Where I disagree is on the remedy: I do not think awarding B027 must spend the whole Cirac-Zoller recognition, because the decisive theory for lattice simulation is the lattice Hubbard proposal and the experiments that realised it, not the gate architecture. Dropping Cirac from my configuration is a direct response to your point. I still see the ion-trap case as a computing architecture whose scalability is unproven, while the lattice work has already delivered a controlled many-body platform, but I agree that Wineland's 2012 prize and the Blatt versus Monroe choice are the weakest points of B015, and I would not block it.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the lattice clock rests on a different principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, that a prize should not wait on the redefinition of the second, and that a citation should be drafted narrowly.
responses.response: I find the magic-wavelength argument persuasive on novelty: engineering the trap so it does not perturb the transition is a different idea from counting optical cycles or controlling single ions, and I agree the redefinition schedule should not decide a prize. This moves B051 up as a fallback for me, and it is now my first alternative. I would still ask whether the benefit lands mostly in metrology and tests of fundamental physics, whereas lattice simulation changes how many-body problems are posed, but I concede that your clean two-name credit is better than mine, and that the same narrow-drafting discipline should apply to my own citation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first, said novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 must be argued, and called the cut among the five lattice-simulation names a genuine difficulty.
responses.response: I agree the cut is genuine and I do not claim to have resolved it; I have only made it explicit, by crediting the proposal plus the first many-body experiment and acknowledging that Cirac, Dalibard and Jaksch are left out. On the clock, your argument that controlling collective and density-dependent shifts made neutral atoms competitive with ions convinces me that it is more than a refinement, so I would vote for B051 over B050 if the committee turns away from my preferred entry, because its credit is the one I can defend most easily.

uncertainties: Whether Zoller, Cirac or Dalibard is the right theory name for lattice simulation, and whether leaving out Jaksch and Cirac is defensible.
Whether the committee will accept B027 as a distinct achievement from the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems.
Whether analogue quantum simulation has yet gone beyond classical simulability enough to count as a mature discovery rather than a promising programme.
I am relying on my own recall of the history of the lattice proposals and experiments and have not verified priority details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the credited candidates appears among my documented supervisors, institutions or co-authors. I work in statistical physics and neural networks, so I have a subject-area interest in many-body models, which is field proximity and not a personal or institutional connection. This is unchanged from round 1.
